## **Post-Construction Bat and Bird Fatality Study Judith Gap Wind Farm Wheatland County, Montana**

## **FINAL REPORT**

**Results from June–October 2009 Study and Comparison with 2006-2007 Study**

## _**Prepared for:**_

Judith Gap Energy LLC

## _**Prepared by:**_

Victoria Poulton, Wallace Erickson **W** estern **E** co **S** ystems **T** echnology **,** Inc. 2003 Central Avenue Cheyenne, Wyoming

## **INTRODUCTION**

The Judith Gap Wind Farm (the “Project”), in Wheatland County consists of 90 1.5-megawatt (MW) turbines.  In 2006, Invenergy established the Judith Gap Energy Center Technical Advisory Committee (TAC) made up of MT Fish, Wildlife and Parks, MT Audubon, Yellowstone Valley Audubon, US Fish and Wildlife Service, Northwestern Energy, and MT Department of Natural Resources and Conservation.  This was based on a recommendation of the July 2004 Environmental Assessment (EA), which produced a Finding of No Significant Impact, meaning that the Judith Gap Energy Center was not likely to have a significant impact on wildlife.  In consultation with the TAC and per the Environmental Assessment, Invenergy contractor TRC Companies, Inc. conducted the first year of mortality monitoring in late summer/fall of 2006 and spring of 2007, and estimated fatality rates of 3.0 birds/MW and 8.9 bats/MW (TRC 2008).

Because the fatality estimate was higher for bats than predicted in the EA (8.9/MW versus 2.5/MW), even though no threatened or endangered species were found, Invenergy conducted an additional year of fatality monitoring in 2009 using standardized carcass searches and carcass removal and searcher efficiency trials.  The objective of this monitoring was to try to validate the fatality estimate prior to trying to either estimate impact (which will require population data) or employing mitigation techniques. Monitoring was conducted from June to October 2009 to monitor breeding bird populations, which were not previously examined, and again monitor migrating bat populations.

The protocol for the fatality monitoring study was similar to protocols used at the Vansycle Project in northeastern Oregon (Erickson et al. 2000), the Stateline project in Oregon and Washington (FPL et al. 2001, Erickson et al. 2003a), the Buffalo Ridge project in southwestern Minnesota (Johnson et al. 2000), the Wild Horse Wind Project in Washington (Erickson et al. 2008), and the Foote Creek Rim project in Wyoming (Young et al. 2003).  The TAC evaluated the methods and results of the monitoring program used in 2006-2007, and recommended changes, including the need for additional monitoring.

This report presents results from the 2009 study, and also includes the results from the 20062007 study as reported in TRC (2008) for comparison.

## **METHODS**

This study was designed to estimate bat and bird fatality at the Project and determine if environmental and other factors influenced mortality rates. Monitoring was conducted for the summer breeding season (June 1 – 15 August) and the fall migration season (16 August – 31 October). The methods were broken into four primary components: 1) standardized carcass searches, 2) searcher efficiency trials, 3) carcass removal trials, and 4) an incidental casualty and injured bird reporting system.

## _**Assumptions**_

Levels of mortality for the wind energy facility as a whole were estimated by searching a predefined area around wind turbine generators and recording all carcasses found. This is accomplished most efficiently by sampling turbines through time and space, so a subset of all possible turbines was searched on a periodic basis. Thus, decisions regarding the number of turbines searched, the specific turbines searched, the total area around specific turbines, and the interval that those turbines are searched influence the estimate of the total number of fatalities attributable to wind turbine operation. Standard statistical procedures account for variance associated with these factors. Another sampling decision that can influence mortality estimates is the size of the search plot. Studies at the Vansycle wind plant (Erickson et al. 2000), the Buffalo Ridge wind plant (Johnson et al. 2002, Higgins et al. 1996), the Foote Creek Rim wind plant (Young et al. 2003), and the Nine Canyon Wind Project (Erickson et al. 2003b) indicate nearly all fatalities are found within the tip height distance measured along the ground from the base of the turbines, with a large majority of bat carcasses found within a distance equal to 50% of the tip height. Bats were of particular concern in this study, so search plots were smaller than those used in previous years.

Factors independent of sampling choices also contribute to uncertainty. Some of these additional factors can also introduce substantial bias into estimates of wind turbine-associated mortality, and must therefore be measured and accounted for. Chief among these are removal of carcasses (e.g., by scavengers) before searchers have opportunity to find them, and carcasses that are present, but missed by searchers. Rates of carcass removal by scavengers are likely to vary with time of year, scavenger density, conspicuousness of carcasses, and other factors. If carcass removal rates are high, then fewer carcasses was available to be found during searches, and mortality estimates was biased low. Trials designed to estimate the rate at which carcasses are removed by scavengers was used to account for this source of bias. Variation in searcher efficiency comes primarily from differences in vegetative condition in search plots, color and disposition of carcasses, and individual searcher skill. Searchers are never 100% efficient, so failure to account for this variability will result in mortality estimates that are biased low. Trials designed to estimate searcher efficiency were used to account for this source of bias.

We assume that levels of background mortality (i.e., mortality not associated with turbines) and crippling bias (mortality of animals injured by turbines but that die from those injuries at a later time) are small. Most fatality monitoring studies at wind-energy facilities have used this approach because of the relative high costs or improbability of obtaining accurate estimates (Smallwood 2007; also see Johnson et al. 2000). However, if either assumption is false, then mortality estimates may be biased high or low, respectively.

## _**Sample Size**_

Thirty of the 90 turbines in the Project were selected for searching using a systematic random sample to ensure that sampled plots were spread throughout the Project site and to allow inference to the project as a whole (Figure 1). Turbine 7 was originally chosen for searching but was not operating after the first round of searches, so Turbine 8 was searched instead for the duration of the study.

## _**Search Plots and Schedule**_

Turbine search plots were 100 m on a side (50 m from the turbine) and centered on the turbine (Figure 2). Studies at wind farms with other large turbines (e.g., Johnson et al. 2003, Young et al. 2005) indicate nearly all fatalities are found within the area that is roughly equivalent to the height of the turbine hub, and most bat fatalities are generally found within an even smaller area around the turbine (Kunz et al. 2007). A smaller search plot was used, which allowed more turbines to be searched. Each plot was searched systematically, with the searcher walking along transects 6-10 meters apart and scanning the ground out to 3-5 meters on either side of the transect. Searchers walked at a rate of approximately 45-60 meters per minute. Transects were closer together where vegetation was dense and impeded visibility. Landcover around searched turbines was either cultivated wheat or grassland (grazed or Conservation Reserve Program [CRP]; Figure 3). Turbines were searched approximately every two weeks.

## _**Carcass Searches**_

The objective of the standardized carcass searches was to systematically search plots at the 30 selected turbines for bat and bird casualties attributable to collision with the turbines. Personnel trained in proper search techniques conducted the carcass searches. The condition of each carcass found was recorded using the following categories:

- Intact - a carcass that is completely intact, is not badly decomposed, and shows no sign of being fed upon by a predator or scavenger.

- Scavenged - an entire carcass, which shows signs of being fed upon by a predator or scavenger, or a portion(s) of a carcass in one location (e.g., wings, skeletal remains, portion of a carcass, etc.), or a carcass that has been heavily infested by insects.

- Feather Spot - 10 or more feathers found at one location indicating predation or scavenging.

All carcasses found were labeled with a unique number, bagged, and frozen for future reference and possible necropsy. A copy of the original data sheet for each carcass was placed in the bag with the frozen carcass. For all casualties found, data recorded included species, sex and age when possible, date and time collected, GPS location, condition (intact, scavenged, feather spot), distance and bearing to turbine, and any comments that may indicate cause of death. All casualties located were photographed as found.

Casualties found by carcass searchers during scheduled searches but outside the formal search area were treated following the above protocol as closely as possible. Bat and bird casualties found in non-search areas (e.g., near a turbine not included in the study or at one of the 30 turbines but at times when searching is not being conducted) were coded as incidental discoveries and documented in a similar fashion to those found during standard searches.

## _**Searcher Efficiency Trials**_

The objective of the searcher efficiency trials was to estimate the percentage of casualties that were found by the observers. Estimates of searcher efficiency were used to correct for detection bias by adjusting the total number of carcasses found for those missed by observers. Searcher efficiency trials were conducted by placing “trial” carcasses in the same areas where carcass searches occur. Efficiency trials were conducted twice during the study. Observers conducting carcass searches did not know which plots would have trial carcasses, the number of trial

carcasses per plot, or the locations of trial carcasses. During each trial, 10 large bird and 10 small bird carcasses were used for a total of 40 searcher-efficiency trial carcasses for the entire study. Carcasses consisted of non-native/non-protected or commercially available species such as rock pigeons ( _Columba livia_ ), hen mallards ( _Anas platyrhynchos_ ), and _Coturnix_ quail. All trial carcasses were placed at random locations within areas being searched prior to the carcass search on the same day. Each trial carcass was discreetly marked so that it would be identified as a trial carcass after it was found. The number and location of the trial carcasses found during the carcass search was recorded and number of carcasses available for detection during each trial was determined immediately after the trial by the person responsible for distributing the carcasses. The efficiency estimate for small birds was also used to estimate searcher efficiency for bats (see Arnett 2008).

## _**Carcass Removal Trials**_

The objective of carcass removal trials was to estimate the length of time fatalities remain in the search area. Estimates of carcass removal were used to adjust carcass counts for removal bias. Carcass removal includes removal by predation or scavenging, or removal by other means such as being plowed into a field.

Two carcass removal trials were conducted during the study. By spreading trials throughout the study period, the effects of varying weather, climatic conditions, and scavenger densities were taken into account. Forty-five small bird carcasses and 22 large bird carcasses were used during both removal trials. Bird carcasses were similar to those used in the searcher efficiency trials were used, and unfrozen carcasses were used in the carcass removal trials to the greatest extent possible.

To minimize the chance of confusing a trial bird with a true casualty, removal trial carcasses were marked discreetly (e.g., with dark electrical tape around one or both legs) for recognition by searchers and other personnel and placed at turbines that were not regularly searched for fatalities. Trial carcasses were randomly located in an area of the same size as search plots.

The observer(s) conducting the trials monitored the trial birds over a 40-day period. Carcasses were checked every day for the first four days, and then on day seven, day ten, day fourteen, and day forty. Carcasses were photographed during checks to document decomposition rates, timing and extent of insect infestations, and rate at which predators/scavengers reduced the carcass to skeletal remains. This information was used to help train searchers in estimation of carcass age. This schedule was followed as closely as possible, but varied depending on weather and coordination with the other survey work. At the end of the 40-day period any remaining evidence of the carcasses was removed.

## Statistical Methods for Fatality Estimates

Estimates of facility-related fatalities are based on:

- (1) Observed number of carcasses found during standardized searches during the monitoring period for which the cause of death was either unknown or was probably facility-related;

- (2) Non-removal rates expressed as the estimated average probability a carcass is expected to remain in the study area and be available for detection by the searchers during removal trials; and

- (3) Searcher efficiency expressed as the proportion of planted carcasses found by searchers during searcher efficiency trials.

The number of bat and bird fatalities attributable to operation of the Judith Gap Wind Farm is based on the number of bat and bird fatalities found whose death appeared related to facility operation, adjusted for removal and searcher efficiency bias.

## **RESULTS**

This report presents new results from the study conducted in 2009, and also supplies results from the 2006-2007 study reported in TRC (2008) for comparison. Search efforts were different between the two studies: in 2006-2007, 20 turbines were searched, using a 195-m plot size and monthly search interval from August to October 2006 and February to May 2007.

## _**Bird Fatalities**_

Twenty-six bird carcasses were recorded during three months of searches in late summer-fall 2006 and four months of searches in spring of 2007 at the Judith Gap Wind Farm (Table 1). Fifteen bird fatalities were found during scheduled carcass searches and 11 were found incidentally, with two incidental finds in July before scheduled searches started, and one incidental find in November after searches had ended. All bird fatalities found during 2006-2007 represented eleven identified species (Table 1). Two raptors were found: a short-eared owl ( _Asio flammeus_ ) during a scheduled carcass search, and a merlin ( _Falco columbarius_ ) as an incidental find near the O&M building. Eared grebe ( _Podiceps nigricollis_ ), horned lark ( _Eremophila alpestris_ ), and American coot ( _Fulica americana_ ) were the most common fatalities found. The number of fatalities per turbine varied from zero at four turbines to three at turbine 32 (Figure 5a). Five turbines had two fatalities during the study, and 10 had one fatality each. Three incidental finds did not appear to be associated with any turbines; two were American coots found on an access road and one was the merlin found near the O&M building.

Bird fatalities were found during all months of searches except for February, and only one was found in March (Figure 6a). The most fatalities (9) were found in September.

Ten bird carcasses were recorded during five months of scheduled searches at the Judith Gap Wind Farm (Table 1, Figure 4). No bird fatalities were found incidentally. Of the bird fatalities, five were horned lark, one was gray partridge ( _Perdix perdix_ ), and four were unidentified birds (Table 1). No raptors or sensitive species were found. The number of bird fatalities per turbine varied from zero at 21 of the searched turbines to two fatalities at turbine 4. Eight turbines had one fatality each (Figure 5b).

All bird fatalities were found in June, July, and August; no bird fatalities were found in September or October (Figure 6b). One bird carcass appeared to be fresh (less than 24 hrs), two

appeared to be 2-3 days old, one appeared to be 4-7 days old, and one was estimated to be more than 2 weeks old. The remaining five did not have time since death estimated; of these, four were feather spots. One bird fatality (a horned lark) was a recent fledgling but did have full flight feathers. All others were adult or did not have age determined.

Over half (six) of the bird fatalities was found less than 30 m from the turbine, two were between 30 and 40 m, and two were between 40 and 50 m of the turbine (Figure 7). Most bird fatalities were found in the northeast (5 fatalities) and northwest (4) quadrants of the turbine search plot. The southwest quadrant had one fatality. Turbine lighting appeared to have no effect on number of bird fatalities – with seven bird fatalities at lit turbines and three at unlit turbines, the difference of the means was 0.279 and the 95% confidence interval was -0.045, 0.603.

## _**Bat Fatalities**_

Thirty-six bat carcasses were found during three months of searches in late summer-fall 2006 and four months of searches in spring of 2007 at the Judith Gap Wind Farm (Table 2). Only one of these bats was found incidentally. Seventeen finds were hoary bats ( _Lasiurus cinereus_ ), four were silver-haired bats ( _Lasionycteris noctivagans_ ), and 15, including the incidental find, were unidentified. The number of bat fatalities per turbine ranged from zero at two turbines to four at turbines 6 and 73 (Figure 5b). Four turbines had three fatalities, four turbines had two fatalities, and eight had one fatality each (Figure 5b).

All bat fatalities but one were found during August, September, and October. One hoary bat was found in mid-May (Figure 6b). Most bat fatalities (25) were found in August.

Twenty bat carcasses were recorded during five months of scheduled searches at the Judith Gap Wind Farm (Table 2, Figure 8). Species found included hoary bat, silver-haired bat, and _Myotis_ sp. (Table 2). An additional four bats were found incidentally. The number of bat fatalities per turbine ranged from zero at 15 turbines to four at turbine 1. Turbine 31 and 8 had two fatalities each, and all other turbines had one bat fatality each (Figure 9).

Bat fatalities were found between June and September; no bat fatalities were found in October (Figure 10). Bat fatalities peaked in late July. Approximately 18% of bat fatalities appeared fresh (less than 24 hrs), 41% appeared to be 2-3 days old, 9% appeared to be 4-7 days old, 5% were between one and two weeks old, and 27% did not have time since death estimated.

Most (91%) of bat fatalities were within 40 m of the turbine (Figure 11). One was between 40 and 50 m of the turbine, and one was more than 60 m from the turbine. Most bat fatalities (10) were found in the southeast quadrant of the search plot, six were in the northeast quadrant, and four each were found in the northwest and southwest quadrants. Turbine lighting appeared to have no effect on number of fat fatalities – with 12 bat fatalities at lit turbines and eight at unlit turbines, the difference of the means was 0.300 and the 95% confidence interval was -0.237, 0.837.

## _**Searcher Efficiency Trials**_

A total of 60 bird carcasses (30 large birds and 30 small birds) were placed in the field during searcher efficiency trials conducted August-October 2006 and March-May 2007 (Table 3). Large birds were placed an average of 7.2 days before the trial search was conducted, and small birds were placed an average of 8.3 days before the trial began. Overall detection rates for large birds was 76.7%, and for small birds the overall detection rate was 16.7%; however, due to the long interval between carcass placement and searching, the small bird detection rate used to adjust for searcher efficiency bias for the 2006-2007 study was 47%. Large bird detection rates were not adjusted. The adjustment for the small bird detection rate was based on carcass removal rate determined during removal trials.

A total of 40 carcasses (20 large birds and 20 small birds) were placed in the field during searcher efficiency trials conducted on two separate dates in 2009 (Table 3). Since no bats were available for searcher efficiency trials, the results for small birds were used for bats. Observer detection rates were 70.0% across both seasons for large birds and 20.0% for small birds and bats (Table 3).

## _**Carcass Removal Trials**_

For carcass removal trials in 2006-2007, 30 large birds and 30 small birds were placed in the field. Removal trials were conducted in August-October 2006 and March-May 2007. For large birds, the average time carcasses remained in the field was 15.4 days, and 23% of large carcasses remained on the 20[th] day of the trial. For small birds, the average time carcasses remained in the field was 9.1 days and 10% remained on the 20[th] day of the trial. Mean carcass residency was shorter during the March-May period (14.7 days for large birds, 5.3 days for small birds) compared to the August-October period (16.3 day for large birds, 13.2 days for small birds).

A total of 67 carcasses (22 large birds, 45 small birds) were placed during two carcass removal trials. Mean removal time for large birds was 10.61 days and mean removal time for small birds was 8.87 days. The second day after placement, 77.3% of large birds and 64.4% of small birds remained in the field (Figure 12). After one week, 54.5% of large birds and 31.1% of small birds still remained, and after two weeks, 40.9% of large birds and 26.7% of small birds remained available for detection (Figure 12).

## _**Adjusted Fatality Estimates**_

Adjusted fatality estimates were calculated the same way for the 2006-2007 study and the 2009 study. The formulas used to calculate adjusted fatality rates for the two studies are written differently in the reports, but function the same.

The adjusted fatality estimate at Judith Gap in 2006-2007 for all birds, accounting for number of turbines searched, searcher efficiency, and scavenger removal, was 3.01/MW/period of study. For large birds, the adjusted fatality estimate was 0.46/MW/period of study, and for small birds it was 0.2.55/MW/period of study. For bats, the adjusted fatality estimate was 8.9/MW/period of study.

The adjusted fatality estimate at Judith Gap Wind Farm in 2009 for all birds, accounting for number of turbines searched, searcher efficiency, and scavenger removal, is 2.22 birds/MW/period of study. For large birds the adjusted fatality estimate is 0.06/large birds/MW/period of study, and for small bird it is 2.16 small birds/MW/period of study. For bats, the adjusted fatality estimate is 4.80 bats/MW/period of study.

## **DISCUSSION**

The 2006-2007 study searched for fatalities over seven months in late summer into fall and again in spring. The 2009 study searched for fatalities during five months in summer and fall. Because of the different durations of the studies, fatalities rates are expressed as number of fatalities per megawatt for the “study period”. Since the study periods are different, the adjusted fatality estimates are not directly comparable, but an attempt is made in this discussion to evaluate reasons for similarities and differences between the two studies.

## _**Bird Fatalities**_

The estimated bird fatality rate was 3.01/MW/period of study in 2006-2007 and 2.22 /MW/period of study in 2009. These bird fatality rates are similar to other wind energy facilities in the Plains states and Midwest where the range of overall bird fatality estimates at seven wind energy projects located in Montana, Wyoming, Nebraska, Wisconsin, Minnesota, Iowa and Illinois has ranged from 0.7 to 3.4 birds/MW/year (Derby et al. 2007; Howe et al. 2002; Johnson et al. 2000, 2002; Jain 2005; Kerlinger et al. 2007, Young et al. 2003). The most common bird species identified among all bird fatalities was horned lark. No species protected by federal or state endangered or threatened species regulations were found during either study.

No one turbine was responsible for a disproportionate number of bird fatalities in either study. Bird fatalities seemed to be well-distributed around the Project, so no part of the Project or group of turbines had unusually high fatalities. Turbines with FAA lighting did not appear to have significantly more fatalities than unlit turbines.

More bird fatalities were found during June in the 2009 study, while bird fatalities were highest in August and September during the 2006-2007 study. Annual fatality rates at Judith Gap are unlikely to be much higher than the rates reported here when both studies are considered together since the months when fatalities have not been studied (November-January) likely have low fatality rates based on the drop-off in fatalities found after September in both studies, and before March in the 2006-2007 study.

The 2006-2007 study detected more species of birds, and waterfowl made up half of all fatalities. Little water is available in the study area, with the only water appearing to be present at a stock impoundment on the southwest side of the Project area. The authors of the 2006-2007 study speculated that waterfowl fatalities were migrants through the area (TRC 2008).

## _**Bat Fatalities**_

The fatality estimate for bats during 2006-2007 was 8.9/MW/study period, and was 4.80 fatalities/MW/year during the 2009 study. No species protected by federal or state endangered or threatened species regulations were found during the 2006-2007 study, and no protected species have been identified among the 2009 fatalities, though not all identifications are confirmed yet. Both studies encompassed the time of year when bat fatalities are highest (July-October). The mathematical average of these two rates is 6.85 fatalities/MW/study, near the low end of the range of bat fatality rates reported for other wind energy projects in North America (Johnson 2005, Arnett et al. 2008), and similar to reported rates from studies conducted in the Plains states and Midwest where bat mortality ranged from 1.16 to 9.82/MW/year (Derby et al. 2007; Howe et al. 2002; Johnson et al. 2000, 2002; Jain 2005; Kerlinger et al. 2007, TRC 2008, Young et al. 2003). To date, the highest fatality estimates for bats have come from the eastern US, particularly the Appalachian region where estimates have ranged from 20.8 to 69.6 bats per turbine or 14.9 to 53.3 bats per MW (Arnett et al. 2008).

Species composition of fatalities at Judith Gap appears to be similar to that at most other wind energy facilities, in that most bat fatalities are hoary bat and silver-haired bat, which are migratory, tree-dwelling species. Based on the timing of fatalities for these species, combined with the lack of forest cover that might provide habitat for resident bats, most were fall migrants through the site, as is the case at virtually all other wind energy facilities in North America (Johnson 2005, Arnett et al. 2008). There are no large expanses of forested areas that would tend to concentrate migrating bats through the Judith Gap Wind Farm, though regional topography shows two mountain ranges to the northeast and northwest of the Project, and migrating bats may prefer to move through the gap between these ranges.

Johnson (2004) summarized data available for 1,628 bat collision fatalities in the U.S. and found that approximately 90% of the fatalities occurred from mid-July through the end of September, with over 50% occurring in August. This study found a similar pattern in bat fatalities, with bat fatalities peaking in late July in the 2009 study and August in the 2006-2007 study. The reported peak of turbine collision fatality in mid-July through August appears to correspond with postbreeding southward migration of Lasiurine species that do not hibernate like many other species of bats in temperate regions (Findley and Jones 1964, Bogan et al. 1996, Fleming and Eby 2003, Cryan 2003).

Bat fatalities were more common at turbines in the southern part of the Project in 2009, but no one turbine was responsible for extremely high numbers of bat fatalities during either study. Turbine 1, 6, and 73 had the most bat fatalities with four carcasses found, while most turbines had zero or one fatality. Studies at wind projects located in the West generally have not indicated a high degree of spatial clustering of fatalities within a project site. There are no clear habitat

changes in the southern part of the Project that help to explain why more fatalities occurred there. FAA lighting on turbines had no significant effect on bat fatalities.

## _**Comparison With 2008 Report**_

Results from this 2009 study indicate lower levels of large bird, overall bird, and bat mortality than was reported by TRC (2008) for fatality monitoring studies conducted in 2006 and 2007 (Table 4). Small bird fatality rates were similar among the two studies. This study had shorter search intervals (two weeks compared to one month) and searched more turbines (30 compared to 20), but plot sizes were smaller (100 x 100 m compared to 190 x 190 m). Carcass removal times were slightly shorter during the 2009 study compared to the 2006-2007 study. Searcher detection rates were similar for large birds, and were lower for small birds, though the detection rate used by TRC (2008) was adjusted higher since the trial birds were placed over eight days before the trial began. Shorter search intervals reduce the effect of fatalities being removed by scavengers before the next search. Shorter carcass removal times increase the adjustments for carcass removal. Lower searcher detection rates result in the fatality rate adjusted upward since it is assumed that the searcher misses more fatalities.

Even though search effort and intensity were higher in 2009, fewer fatalities were found and both observed and adjusted fatality rates were lower in 2009 compared to the 2006-2007 study (Table 4 and 5). Lower bird fatalities in 2009 may be partly due to smaller search plots, but most bat fatalities in 2006-2007 were found within 50 m, which was the area searched in 2009.  Fewer bird species were found in 2009 (two species) compared to 2006-2007 (11 species; Table 5). No raptors were found in 2009, compared to two found in 2006-2007 (a short-eared owl and a merlin). Waterfowl were common fatalities found in 2006-2007 (13 or 50% of individuals representing four species), but none were found in 2009. Searcher detection rates do not appear to be responsible for this difference in fatality numbers since actual detection rates were similar for the two projects (Table 4) and waterfowl generally are easy to spot in the field since they are large bodied and tend to persist longer. The difference in species found during the two studies is likely a real difference, not an artifact of sampling methods. Environmental conditions such as amount of precipitation, temperatures, wind, or land use changes may have contributed to the difference in species found between the two studies.

Bird and bat results are likely comparable between the two studies during the months of August, September, and October since carcass removal trials and searcher efficiency trials attempt to reconcile differences in search effort. The 2009 study found the most bat fatalities during July, but searches did not take place in July of 2006, so that study may have missed an important number of bat fatalities. The estimated bat fatality rate for the 2009 study period is probably representative of fatality rates for that year since the 2009 likely captured at least 90% of annual bat fatalities (Johnson 2004).
